Guthuk Noodle Soup

Served at: Losar (Tibetan New Year)

Serves 6-8Prep 45 minCook 1 hour 15 min

Guthuk is a traditional Tibetan noodle soup eaten on Losar Eve, the day before Tibetan New Year. This hearty and symbolic dish is central to the Nyi Shu Gu (29th day) celebrations, where the hidden ingredients within the dough dumplings offer playful predictions and reflections on the coming year for those who find them. It's a time for family to gather, share laughter, and cleanse away the old year's misfortunes.

Ingredients

  • For the Dough:
  • 2 cups (240g) all-purpose flour
  • 1/2 teaspoon salt
  • 3/4 cup (180ml) warm water, or as needed
  • For the Soup:
  • 1 tablespoon vegetable oil
  • 1 pound (450g) lamb or beef, cut into 1-inch (2.5 cm) cubes
  • 8 cups (1.9 L) beef or vegetable broth
  • 1 large daikon radish (about 1 lb / 450g), peeled and diced into 1/2-inch (1.2 cm) pieces
  • 2 carrots, peeled and sliced
  • 1 cup (75g) chopped spinach or bok choy
  • 2 cloves garlic, minced
  • 1 inch (2.5 cm) fresh ginger, grated
  • 1 teaspoon salt, or to taste
  • 1/2 teaspoon black pepper, or to taste
  • Optional: 2 tablespoons soy sauce
  • For the Symbolic Fillings (small, clean pieces):
  • A small piece of wool (for kindness)
  • A small piece of charcoal (for ill will, or a dark bean as substitute)
  • A small dried chili pepper (for a sharp tongue)
  • A small pebble (for stubbornness)
  • A small coin (for prosperity)
  • A small pinch of salt (for laziness)
  • A small piece of paper with a sun or moon drawn on it (for good fortune)

Method

  1. Prepare the Dough: In a large bowl, combine flour and salt. Gradually add warm water, mixing until a shaggy dough forms. Turn onto a lightly floured surface and knead for 5-7 minutes until smooth and elastic. Cover with a damp cloth and let rest for at least 30 minutes.
  2. Prepare the Symbolic Fillings: While the dough rests, gather and prepare your symbolic items.
  3. Shape the Guthuk: Divide the dough into small, walnut-sized pieces. Roll each piece into a thin, flat disc or an irregular shape. For some pieces, carefully insert one symbolic item into the center and seal the dough tightly around it, ensuring the item is completely hidden. Leave most dough pieces plain.
  4. Brown the Meat: Heat vegetable oil in a large pot or Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Add the lamb or beef cubes and brown them on all sides. Remove meat and set aside.
  5. Build the Broth: Add minced garlic and grated ginger to the pot and sauté for 1 minute until fragrant. Pour in the broth and bring to a boil. Return the browned meat to the pot, reduce heat to low, cover, and simmer for 45 minutes to 1 hour, or until the meat is tender.
  6. Add Vegetables: Add diced daikon radish and sliced carrots to the soup. Simmer for 10-15 minutes, or until vegetables are tender-crisp. Stir in the spinach or bok choy and cook for another 2-3 minutes until wilted.
  7. Cook the Guthuk: Gently drop the prepared dough pieces (guthuk), both plain and those with fillings, into the simmering soup. Cook for 5-7 minutes, or until they float to the surface and are cooked through.
  8. Season and Serve: Season the soup with salt, pepper, and soy sauce (if using) to taste. Ladle hot Guthuk into individual bowls, ensuring each person receives some of the special dough pieces. Enjoy the fun of discovering the hidden symbols!

Tips

  • Ensure all symbolic items are thoroughly cleaned before being enclosed in the dough. For charcoal, a dark bean or lentil can be a safe and symbolic substitute.
  • The dough pieces can be made ahead of time. Lightly flour them to prevent sticking and store them on a baking sheet in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours.
  • For a vegetarian version, omit the meat and use vegetable broth. Add mushrooms, tofu, or chickpeas for extra texture and protein.
